newsitem.title: USA: Former Evergreen execs settle SEC suit.
newsitem.headline: Former Evergreen execs settle SEC suit.

text.p: Two former executives of the defunct Evergreen Information Technologies Inc have settled charges with the Securities and Exchange Commission regarding faulty reporting and misuse of company funds, the agency said Tuesday.
It said company founder Barry Nelsen, 49, and former Chief Financial Officer Ellis Tallant, 68, agreed to settle the charges without admitting or denying wrongdoing.

In a complaint filed in U.S. District Court here, the SEC alleged Nelsen misappropriated company funds and arranged for Evergreen to make illegal political contributions when the U.S. Department of the Navy refused to provide certain computer information the McLean, Va., company needed in order to develop its database.
"In a vain effort to convince the Navy to change its mind, Nelsen solicited Evergreen employees to contribute to the campaign committee or organizations of certain members of Congress," the SEC said.
Tallant was accused by the SEC of signing the company's initial public offering documents while knowing some of the information being disclosed was wrong.

The company's product, called "Powertree," was to be an interactive database providing virtually all of the regulations and specifications market participants would need to produce and sell products and services to the federal government.
The SEC alleged Nelsen solicited Evergreen employees to write personal checks totalling $20,000 in amounts of $1,000 and he later illegally reimbursed them with company funds.
The agency alleged that Tallant and Nelsen signed the company's 1992 initial public offering statement while knowing it contained faulty information.
It also alleged that Nelsen knowingly signed a false Evergreen quarterly report for the period ended August 31, 1992.
Evergreen ceased operating in July 1994. From its inception, the company had no significant revenues and incurred a cumulative net loss of $7.9 million.
Nelsen was waived from paying any penalties based on his financial condition, but has agreed to be banned from serving as an officer or director of a public company, the SEC said.
Tallant has agreed to a $20,000 penalty, it said.
Neither Tallant or Nelsen could be reached for comment on the settlement.
